title: South Korea’s AI Power Under Uneven Interdependence
subtitle: Semiconductor Depth, National Conversion, and the KIC Model-Selection Case
full_title: South Korea’s AI Power Under Uneven Interdependence: Semiconductor Depth, National Conversion, and the KIC Model-Selection Case

creators.name: Wu, Shaoyuan
creators.affiliation: Global AI Governance and Policy Research Center, EPINOVA LLC

publisher_unit: Global AI Governance and Policy Research Center
description: This policy brief examines South Korea’s AI power under uneven technological interdependence. It argues that Korea combines globally consequential semiconductor and high-bandwidth-memory capabilities with growing domestic models, public compute programs, cloud and telecommunications capacity, and industrial and administrative AI applications, but these strengths do not constitute a nationally controlled end-to-end AI stack. The brief distinguishes AI National Power, AI Boundary Power, Boundary Autonomy, and Systemic Influence, and evaluates Korea’s capacity conversion across memory, compute, domestic models, industrial AI, and public-sector deployment. It uses the Korea Investment Corporation as a diagnostic case of mixed-origin institutional AI, where Chinese-developed Qwen3 and BGE-M3 reportedly operate alongside U.S.-developed models for differentiated internal functions. The case does not establish foreign control, strategic realignment, or durable dependence; instead, it highlights the importance of deployment architecture, continuing control rights, switching costs, security review, and function-preserving substitution. The brief concludes that South Korea’s future AI power will depend on converting specialized technological depth into sustainable national functions, exercising effective control at consequential interfaces, and preserving credible alternatives under disruption.
abstract: South Korea combines globally consequential AI-memory manufacturing with domestic models, public-private compute allocation, advanced cloud and telecommunications organizations, and manufacturing applications. These strengths do not comprise a nationally controlled end-to-end AI stack. Advanced accelerators, semiconductor equipment, packaging relationships, model software, and overseas production sites create external interfaces over which Korean actors exercise only partial authority. The analytical question is how Korean institutions convert heterogeneous resources into functions they can access and sustain, while retaining credible alternatives where consequential interfaces are controlled elsewhere. KIC provides a diagnostic institutional case. Its reported use of Chinese-developed language and retrieval models is compatible with substantial domestic model-development capacity and close U.S.-linked semiconductor and security relationships. Yet reported use volumes, the timing of its GPU expansion contract, and unknown system architecture prevent strong claims about which models are operationally indispensable, whether foreign actors possess continuing technical control, or whether cross-border adoption has become systemic influence. The practical implication is not model-origin neutrality at any cost: it is function-based procurement subject to verifiable security, legal, and continuity controls.

methodology.core_problem: How specialized technological depth is converted into nationally usable and sustainable functions under externally controlled interfaces and uneven technological interdependence.
evidence_rules: Available boundary-control capacity, exercised control, and observed target effects are coded separately.
Operating or repeatedly allocated capacity is distinguished from procured resources, infrastructure under construction, announced partnerships, and policy objectives.
Official and corporate claims are attributed to their publishers rather than treated as independent evaluations.
The KIC case is diagnostic and not a representative sample of Korean public-sector procurement.

key_findings: South Korea possesses substantial specialized AI capacity, but national conversion remains uneven.
Strategic supply-chain importance does not automatically translate into AI Boundary Power.
KIC demonstrates mixed-origin model adoption without establishing foreign control or durable dependence.
Boundary Autonomy depends on verified function-preserving substitution rather than supplier diversity alone.
South Korea’s future AI power depends on converting specialized resources into sustainable functions, effective interface control, and credible alternatives under disruption.
policy_recommendations: Register critical AI functions and map models, data flows, licenses, operators, update privileges, and hosting jurisdictions.
Benchmark Korean and foreign models on the same authorized tasks, hardware budgets, security tests, and total operating costs.
Run model and embedding replacement exercises and supplier-interruption tests for critical workflows.
Report public-compute maturity using GPU type, allocable hours, admission rules, queue time, utilization, outages, and unique project identifiers.
Review named HBM, equipment, and model-service interfaces for functional substitutes and external restrictions.
